title: A Hexagonal Galactic Center
caption: The barred lenticular galaxy NGC 7020, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/H. Dottori, R. J. Díaz, G. Gimeno · Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: In this Gemini South image, the center of NGC 7020 has a subtle but unmistakable six-sided shape. NGC 7020 is a barred lenticular galaxy in Pavo, a constellation of the southern sky. Flanking the hexagon to the left and right are two denser clumps of stars, called ansae.

A hexagon is an uncommon shape for any object in space, and rarer still for a whole galaxy. To build one, a large number of stars must follow orbits confined to a very narrow band, and the ansae are part of that orbital path. The unusual shape seems to come from a very rare orbital resonance, or from some phenomenon not yet understood. An orbital resonance happens when orbits fall into a regular, repeating relationship, which can herd objects into distinct patterns.
The 8-meter Gemini South telescope stands on Cerro Pachón in the Chilean Andes. Together with its partner, Gemini North in Hawai‘i, it gives astronomers a deep view of the whole night sky.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini South through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, bringing out the subtle hexagonal shape of the core.
